subject: Immunology
vignette: A 5-year-old boy has recurrent bronchitis and pneumonia. Work-up shows normal immunoglobulin levels, a normal CD4+ count, but a markedly reduced CD8+ T-cell count. Bone marrow and T-cell receptor studies are unrevealing. His circulating T cells are found to be unable to recognize viral peptides displayed on the surface of his virus-infected respiratory epithelium.
question: Which of the following cell types would normally present viral peptides to his CD8+ T cells?

options.text: Only dendritic cells and macrophages, since other cells cannot activate CD8+ T cells
Mast cells, via IgE-bound surface receptors
Any nucleated cell of the body via MHC class I
Erythrocytes, which are the principal source of MHC class I
CD4+ helper T cells, which take up viral proteins from the cytosol

explanation_correct: MHC class I is expressed on the surface of all nucleated cells of the body, not just on professional antigen-presenting cells. That distributed expression lets any infected cell display fragments of viral proteins from its cytosol, so a CD8+ cytotoxic T cell can survey every cell in the body and eliminate infected ones. Dendritic cells are special not because of class I expression but because they additionally express class II and costimulatory molecules and can cross-present antigen, which is why they prime naive CD8+ T cells even though infected tissue cells are the actual targets.

explanation_incorrect.A: Professional antigen-presenting cells are uniquely able to activate naive T cells, but all nucleated cells display class I and can present endogenous viral peptides.
explanation_incorrect.B: Mast cells participate in type I hypersensitivity through IgE and Fc epsilon RI and are not the cells that present viral peptides to CD8+ T cells.
explanation_incorrect.D: Erythrocytes lack a nucleus and therefore lack MHC class I; protein presentation requires a nucleated cell.
explanation_incorrect.E: CD4+ T cells are class II-restricted helpers rather than primary presenters of cytosolic viral peptides to CD8+ T cells.

educationalObjective: MHC class I is found on all nucleated cells, allowing any infected cell to be surveyed by CD8+ cytotoxic T cells.

subject: Immunology
vignette: A 38-year-old woman has recurrent sinopulmonary infections and a chronic granulomatous skin disease. Flow cytometry shows markedly reduced MHC class I on all of her cells despite a normal heavy chain and normal beta-2 microglobulin protein. Genetic sequencing demonstrates a loss-of-function mutation in the TAP1 subunit.
question: Which of the following best explains why MHC class I cannot reach the surface in this patient?

options.text: TAP degrades the invariant chain to permit class I peptide loading
TAP transports the peptide for MHC class II loading in the endosome
TAP transfers intact proteins from the cytosol into lysosomes instead of the ER
TAP transports cytosolic peptides into the ER that stabilize class I, allowing its release from the peptide-loading complex
TAP acts as the chaperone calnexin and folds the class I heavy chain

explanation_correct: TAP (transporter associated with antigen processing) is a heterodimer of TAP1 and TAP2 in the endoplasmic reticulum membrane that pumps cytosolic peptides into the ER lumen. There the peptides meet the peptide-loading complex, containing the class I heavy chain, beta-2 microglobulin, calreticulin, calnexin, and tapasin, and stable peptide binding triggers release and trafficking to the surface. Without TAP, class I molecules remain empty and unstable in the ER, which is why TAP deficiency causes low surface class I, impaired CD8+ responses, and granulomatous skin disease.

explanation_incorrect.A: Invariant chain (CLIP) processing belongs to the class II pathway and requires endosomal cathepsins, not TAP.
explanation_incorrect.B: Class II peptides arise in endosomes and are loaded with the help of HLA-DM and HLA-DO, not delivered by TAP.
explanation_incorrect.C: TAP has no role in transporting intact proteins into lysosomes; that is a property of phagocytosis and endocytosis.
explanation_incorrect.E: Calnexin is a separate chaperone protein that assists class I folding; TAP is a peptide pump, not a chaperone.

educationalObjective: TAP pumps cytosolic peptides into the ER to stabilize MHC class I, which is why TAP-deficiency abolishes surface class I expression.

subject: Immunology
vignette: A 55-year-old man with newly diagnosed melanoma is treated with pembrolizumab, an anti-PD-1 antibody. Despite a strong response, his tumors later recur. Tumor sequencing reveals an acquired homozygous deletion of the beta-2 microglobulin gene in the recurrent lesion.
question: Loss of beta-2 microglobulin most likely allows this tumor to escape which of the following?

options.text: Cytotoxic CD8+ T-cell recognition via MHC class I
Natural killer cell recognition
CD4+ helper T-cell recognition via MHC class II
IgG-mediated antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity
Complement-dependent cytotoxicity by donor antibodies

explanation_correct: Class I-restricted presentation depends on a heavy chain plus beta-2 microglobulin, and beta-2 microglobulin is encoded on chromosome 15, outside the HLA locus, so a single gene loss can silence surface class I across the tumor. With class I absent, tumor peptides are no longer displayed, so tumor-specific CD8+ T cells that were driving the response no longer see their target. Such tumors are functionally invisible to the cytotoxic arm, although the absence of class I eliminates the 'self' signal that restrains natural killer cells, making them more vulnerable to NK-mediated killing, which is a mechanism under study in immunotherapy.

explanation_incorrect.B: Losing class I tends to make cells more, not less, susceptible to natural killer cell killing, because NK cells are inhibited by self class I.
explanation_incorrect.C: CD4+ T-cell recognition uses class II, which does not require beta-2 microglobulin, so class II presentation would be preserved.
explanation_incorrect.D: Antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity and complement do not require MHC class I; the tumor's described escape is T-cell mediated.
explanation_incorrect.E: Complement-mediated lysis depends on the membrane attack complex and has no dependence on beta-2 microglobulin.

educationalObjective: Tumors can escape CD8+ cytotoxic T cells by losing beta-2 microglobulin and thus all surface MHC class I, at the cost of increased NK susceptibility.

subject: Immunology
vignette: A 31-year-old man with HIV infection has been off antiretroviral therapy and now has a rising viral load despite an early strong CD8+ T-cell response. Viral sequencing shows a single amino acid substitution at position 2 of a 9-residue epitope that had been recognized by his HLA-B57-restricted cytotoxic T cells. The mutated virus is no longer killed by these T cells.
question: Which of the following best explains why this single substitution abolished T-cell recognition?

options.text: MHC class I has an open-ended groove that accommodates peptides of 13 to 25 residues, so a single change cannot matter
The mutation blocked proteasomal cleavage of the whole viral polyprotein, preventing any epitope generation
The mutation prevented association of the class I heavy chain with beta-2 microglobulin in all infected cells
MHC class I has a closed groove that binds peptides about 8 to 10 residues long, and the position 2 substitution alters an anchor residue needed for stable binding
The mutation converted the epitope into a peptide that is now presented on MHC class II to CD4+ T cells

explanation_correct: MHC class I binds short peptides, generally 8 to 10 amino acids, in a groove closed at both ends, so specific anchor residues at defined positions determine binding; position 2 and the C-terminal residue are the classic primary anchors for HLA-B57. A substitution at such an anchor weakens or abolishes peptide binding and surface display, so the CD8+ T-cell receptor no longer sees its target, which is a mechanism of viral immune escape. This contrasts with MHC class II, whose open groove accepts longer peptides of roughly 13 to 25 residues with fewer positional constraints.

explanation_incorrect.A: The open-ended groove with longer peptides describes MHC class II, not class I, so this option reverses the two pathways.
explanation_incorrect.B: A single substitution within an epitope does not block proteasomal processing of the whole polyprotein; processing still generates the epitope, but the peptide no longer binds class I.
explanation_incorrect.C: Association of heavy chain with beta-2 microglobulin is a general assembly step unaffected by one peptide's sequence, and it would not selectively eliminate this epitope.
explanation_incorrect.E: Shifting presentation to class II would not explain the loss of killing by his class I-restricted CD8+ T cells, and class II loading requires endosomal delivery.

educationalObjective: MHC class I binds 8-10 residue peptides in a closed groove, so anchor-residue mutations can abolish presentation and allow cytotoxic T-cell escape.
